title: How the web works
subtitle: Type a URL, press Enter — and a dozen systems cooperate in under a second. Follow one request all the way.

sections.title: URLs and clients/servers
sections.body: The web is a client–server system: a browser (client) requests resources from a web server. A URL such as https://example.com:443/docs?page=2#top has scheme (protocol), host, port, path, query string and fragment. The fragment never leaves the browser.

choices.text: A fragment used only by the browser.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is not sent to the server.

sections.title: DNS: names to addresses
sections.body: Computers route by IP address, so the browser first asks DNS to resolve the host name. The answer is cached at several levels (browser, OS, resolver) for its TTL, so repeat visits skip the lookup.

choices.text: How long an answer may be cached.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — DNS lookup
figures.note: The resolver does the legwork and caches the answer.

sections.title: HTTP request and response
sections.body: HTTP is a text protocol: the client sends a request (method, path, headers, optional body); the server answers with a response (status code, headers, body). Methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE. Status families: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone; cookies and tokens carry identity.

choices.text: The resource was not found (client error).

figures.caption: Figure 1.3.1 — loading a page
figures.note: One page view is many round trips.

sections.title: Why latency matters
sections.body: Each round trip costs the network RTT. A page needing DNS (1 RTT), TCP (1), TLS (1–2), then the request (1) needs about 4–5 RTTs before the first byte. HTTP/2 multiplexes requests on one connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC to cut handshakes.

worked.why: RTT = 50 ms. Steps: DNS, TCP, TLS, request = 4 round trips.

questions.prompt: The best way to cut page-load time on a high-RTT link is…

choices.text: Fewer round trips (cache, reuse connections, bundle).

problems.prompt: RTT is 80 ms. A fresh page needs DNS, TCP, TLS (2 RTT) and the GET. Minimum time to first byte?

sections.title: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
sections.body: HTML is structure (headings, links, forms); CSS is presentation (layout, colour); JavaScript is behaviour. The browser parses HTML into the DOM tree, CSS into a style tree, combines them to lay out and paint. Keep the three separate so each can change alone.

questions.prompt: Which layer changes a button’s colour?

sections.title: Static, dynamic and SPA
sections.body: Static sites serve the same files to all; dynamic sites build pages per request on the server; single-page apps (SPAs) load one page and update it with JavaScript, fetching JSON. SPAs feel fast after first load but cost a heavy first load and need care for SEO.

choices.text: A full HTML page for every click.
JSON data, then updates the page in the browser.
